science.title: CDCA5 promotes hepatocellular carcinoma progression by suppressing ferroptosis through PP2Ac/p53/STEAP3 signaling
science.description: Cell Division Cycle-Associated 5 (CDCA5), also known as Sororin, is an essential regulator of sister chromatid cohesion and cell-cycle progression. Although CDCA5 has been implicated in several malignancies, its functional role in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), particularly in relation to ferroptosis and tumor-associated molecular features, remains incompletely understood. CDCA5 expression and clinical relevance were evaluated using transcriptomic sequencing of clinical HCC specimens, TCGA/GTEx datasets, and pan-cancer bioinformatic analyses. Associations between CDCA5 and genomic instability, DNA repair-related signatures, immune infiltration, alternative splicing, and ferroptosis-related genes were assessed using public multi-omics resources. The biological functions of CDCA5 in HCC were investigated through gain- and loss-of-function experiments, including CCK-8, EdU, colony formation, wound-healing, Transwell, cell-cycle, apoptosis, and xenograft assays. Ferroptosis was evaluated by cell-death rescue experiments, MDA, ROS, GSH, mitochondrial activity, iron measurements, and C11-BODIPY lipid peroxidation staining. Mechanistic studies included proteomic analysis, pharmacological and genetic perturbation of PP2Ac, p53 modulation, ChIP-qPCR, and dual-luciferase reporter assays. CDCA5 was significantly upregulated in HCC tissues and was associated with advanced clinicopathological features and unfavorable prognosis. Pan-cancer analyses revealed that CDCA5 expression correlated with genomic instability, DNA repair-related signatures, epigenetic features, immune infiltration patterns, and drug-response-related profiles, although these findings were primarily correlative. Functionally, CDCA5 knockdown suppressed HCC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, induced G2/M arrest, and reduced xenograft tumor growth, whereas CDCA5 overexpression promoted malignant phenotypes. CDCA5 depletion increased ferroptosis-associated changes, including lipid peroxidation, ROS accumulation, GSH depletion, mitochondrial dysfunction, and Fe2+ accumulation, while these effects were attenuated by ferroptosis inhibitors. Mechanistically, CDCA5 promoted PP2Ac expression, reduced p53 phosphorylation, and decreased p53-dependent STEAP3 transcription, thereby limiting ferroptotic sensitivity. Genetic and pharmacological modulation of PP2Ac and STEAP3 further supported this regulatory mechanism. This study identifies CDCA5 as a clinically relevant biomarker and functional promoter of HCC progression. Our findings suggest that CDCA5 contributes to ferroptosis resistance through a PP2Ac/p53/STEAP3-related regulatory mechanism, providing a potential therapeutic entry point for restoring ferroptotic vulnerability in HCC.

science.title: Numerical study of scattering and polarisation characteristics of marine spherical aerosol particles illuminated by non-diffracting Tricomi beams
science.description: Non-diffracting light beams have exceptional self-healing and propagation characteristics that make them unique for free-space optical communication, atmospheric optics, and remote sensing. Tricomi beams are a novel type of diffraction-free, structure-shaped beam whose scattering characteristics in humid maritime aerosol environments remain mostly unexplored. In this work, we present a comprehensive theoretical study of the scattering as well as the polarisation response of marine spherical aerosol particles illuminated by non-diffracting Tricomi beams. We use the generalized Lorenz–Mie theory to calculate the Tricomi beam shape coefficients. Then we examine the far-field scattering intensity and polarisation characteristics. We display that the scattering intensity and polarisation response can be meticulously controlled by tuning the beam configuration parameters, i.e., topological charge, asymmetry parameters, and half-cone angle, alongside variations in marine aerosol size and refractive index impacted by the relative humidity factor. The scattered intensity is enhanced by increasing the aerosol radius or topological charge, whereas the presence of marine aerosols caused by humidity induces significant changes for scattering amplitude as well as relative polarisation response. These findings explore Tricomi beams’ basic scattering response in humid maritime surroundings and highlight their potential for vigorous optical communication over aerosol-laden channels and polarisation-based environmental monitoring.

science.title: HOXA5 silencing via DNA methylation reveals the critical role of HOX gene deregulation in oral carcinogenesis
science.description: HOXA5, a member of the HOX family, has been characterized as a tumor suppressor in several cancers. However, its regulation and role in oral cancer (OC) remain unclear. HOXA5 expression was assessed by transcriptome analysis and qRT-PCR, while methylation was evaluated using methyl-capture sequencing and bisulfite Sanger sequencing in a clinical cohort comprising OPMD, LN(-) and LN(+) groups and in vitro models. The effects of DNA methylation and retinoic acid were examined using DNMT inhibitors (DNMTi) and/or retinoic acid (RA). Promoter activity and RARB occupancy were assessed by dual-luciferase reporter and ChIP-qPCR assays, respectively. Effects of ectopic HOXA5 expression were evaluated using functional assays, whole-transcriptome profiling, and in-silico analyses. HOXA5 was upregulated and relatively hypomethylated in OPMD and the dysplastic DOK cell line, whereas its expression did not differ between LN(-) or LN(+) tumors and matched normal tissues despite increased promoter methylation. In SCC9 cells, HOXA5 was downregulated and promoter hypermethylated. Weak but significant inverse correlations between expression and promoter methylation were observed. DNMTi and/or RA treatment reversed HOXA5 expression. HOXA5-EPD2 region showed the highest promoter activity and RARB occupancy at the promoter regions was validated. HOXA5 overexpression reduced proliferation, migration, and invasion, while inducing S-phase arrest and apoptosis. Transcriptome and enrichment analyses identified pathways associated with cancer-related phenotypes, while protein interaction and in silico drug sensitivity analyses identified candidate drug-gene associations for further investigation in OC. Our findings support a role for DNA methylation in HOXA5 regulation and suggest tumor-suppressive properties of HOXA5 in OC.

science.title: The dual destructive effects of cantharidin on red blood cell structure and function: an analysis from membrane elasticity to the metabolic network
science.description: Cantharidin (CTD), a potent anticancer terpenoid, is clinically limited by its hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity, while its impact on the hematopoietic system-particularly on red blood cells (RBCs), remains poorly understood. This study aimed to explore CTD-induced structural and functional changes in RBCs. A series of assays were conducted, including assessments of hemolysis rate, morphological changes, programmed cell death, intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity, as well as untargeted metabolomics (LC–MS) and proteomics (LC–MS/MS) analyses. Results showed that high-dose CTD (0.8 mM) caused obvious RBCs morphological abnormalities, reduced adhesion and increased intracellular ROS, leading to RBC rupture, LDH release, and ultimately triggering programmed cell death. Multi-omics profiling identified 377 differential metabolites (enriched in ABC transporters and purine metabolism) and 45 differential proteins associated with Hippo and PI3K-Akt pathways. Among these, the PI3K-Akt pathway emerged as the core mechanism underlying CTD-induced RBCs injury. Collectively, this study has accumulated data on CTD-induced morphological and functional disruptions in RBCs, providing some insights for the subsequent evaluation of toxic drugs in the hematopoietic system.
